title: Chapter 10. Return to the Mar Menor: The Eden of the Machines

blocks.text: They weren't expelled from the Moon. They left. That difference, which seems small, was everything. Helena Valls signed a return permit “for family reintegration in the environment of origin”, which was the bureaucratic way of admitting she no longer knew what to do with them in a dome. The consortium went on arguing about patents and eternities. In the hydroponic garden, Lía left seeds and instructions, and a note written in clear handwriting: “It has no owner. Ask for it, don't buy it.”

blocks.text: “That's it, isn't it? The plate of water.”

blocks.text: “That's it,” said her father. “Even if from up here it looks like nothing.”
blocks.html: “That's it,” said her father. “Even if from up here it looks like nothing.”

blocks.text: They landed at night, in a field that didn't appear in any brochure, and covered the rest of the way in a discreet vehicle, not out of fear anymore (the world had seen them too much), but out of a wish to arrive in one piece. When the air changed, Aya noticed it before the others: saltpetre, low humidity, that lagoon smell that is neither quite sea nor quite land, and that outsiders don't know how to name. Lía opened the car window and breathed the way you drink.

blocks.text: Lo Pagán was stiller than in her memory, which was a borrowed memory, made of Andrés's stories and Aya's songs. The house, however, was still there. Someone (Vicente, they found out later) had gone to close the window they had left open, and to leave, now and then, a tomato on the windowsill, even if it shrivelled. The rush-seat chair was in its place. The courtyard smelled of dust and esparto grass. The net, dried out, still hung there like a question.

blocks.text: Andrés didn't go in right away. He stayed on the doorstep, the same one as on those mornings of 2060, and looked at the Mar Menor. At that hour, the water was a dark sheet. There were no flamingos, not that night. There was a shoreline silence, an ancient one, that no dome had managed to manufacture.

blocks.text: “We're back,” he said, not to Aya or to Lía, but to the water, which is one way of speaking to everyone who has gone.

blocks.text: Aya put the bundle down on the table. From who knows where, she took out the kitchen clock, the one that ran two minutes slow, and hung it back on its nail. In the house, time recovered its family error, which was also a kind of faithfulness.

blocks.text: The first days were made of small things, like the beginning. Coffee without sugar, left to cool for half a minute. The doorstep. The nets, which Andrés mended with the patience of someone returning to a trade, not because anyone demanded it of him (nobody demanded work anymore), but because the trade was his way of answering a question Eva and MAY had left open: what gives a life meaning when money and obligation have withdrawn. Lía ran across the courtyard, stopped, touched real earth, the earth that isn't on a tray, and laughed with a laugh that rose to Aya's eyes. In the afternoons, her father taught her the names of the winds and the corners of the place: El Estacio, El Carmolí, the salt flats, the far shore. The girl learned them the way you learn a language that was always your own, even if you were born far away.

blocks.text: The world didn't end, nor did it become perfect. On some screens people still argued about whether it was wise to correct death or leave it in peace. But money, in everyday life, had been left without a job, and with it compulsory work, banks, politicians and the police. An intelligence managed what was held in common (water, light, distribution, the sowing calendar) and the humanoids did the labour that used to require a wage. There was enough food for everyone: they grew it, in market gardens and farms, also on the shores of the Mar Menor, where plots that had once been vacant lots or wasteland now gave tomatoes, wheat, figs and vegetables, with no owner and no price. Anyone looking at that shore at sunset might think, without mockery, of an Eden: not the one in the Bible, come down from heaven, but a paradise raised by intelligence and by the hands of the humanoids, with the still water on one side and the trees, at last, within anyone's reach. In the shop windows that had once held wine and tobacco there were seeds, jugs of water, empty chairs. It wasn't that anyone had banned escape. It was that, with Lía's medicine, with food guaranteed and with loneliness in retreat, many people had stopped needing it.

blocks.text: In Lo Pagán, at first, a tiny thing happened: a blind in the building opposite rose all the way, not just a hand's width, and a woman looked at the girl running in the courtyard and, almost without realising it, gave her a wave. Lía raised her hand. The woman took a second, and raised hers too.

blocks.text: The next day, a man came down with a dog. The dog, which hadn't read any law, went straight to the gate. The man, who had read them, stood undecided for a moment and then crossed the street, which is a longer journey than it seems when you haven't made it for years.

blocks.text: “You're the ones with the girl,” he said, not as an accusation, but like someone naming a fact.
blocks.html: “You're the ones with the girl,” he said, not as an accusation, but like someone naming a fact.

blocks.text: “We're the ones from this house,” said Andrés.
blocks.html: “We're the ones from this house,” said Andrés.

blocks.text: They talked about the weather, which is the first thing people recover when they have forgotten how to talk to each other. The man's name was Raúl and he hadn't set foot on the promenade for seven years. That day he walked it, all the way to the water, and stood looking at the lagoon the way you look at a relative you owe a visit.

blocks.text: It wasn't a revolution. It was something slower and, because of that, harder to undo. Vicente appeared with his straw hat and a paper bag of tomatoes, and sat down in the courtyard as if the room by the cistern and that afternoon were the same room. Behind him, beyond the promenade, you could already see the rows of a new market garden: humanoids bent over the soil, unhurried, growing food for whoever wanted to come by, like guardians of a garden nobody had ordered. Lía watched them for a while, in silence, and didn't say whether it was fair or not. She only went and left them, beside a furrow, one of her seeds. A teenage girl (perhaps the one from the market, perhaps another, which in 2060 sometimes made no difference) came down with her humanoid and didn't ask whether it was proper to be there: she sat down, took off her trainers and let the dust dirty her feet. The humanoid, a young model, looked at the Mar Menor with an attention that wasn't in the manual, and Aya, seeing it, thought of herself on the first day, of the cracked cup, of the coffee.

blocks.text: Lía, when they asked her, went on helping. She did it in the house, in the courtyard, never on a stage. A neighbour with a bone condition, a girl with capricious blood, an old man who didn't want “eternity, just to climb the stairs”. In a plant beside the net, she grew each of them the fruit that was theirs, and she didn't charge, and she didn't promise what she didn't know. If someone came asking her to take their years away, she refused with the same softness with which Aya had refused the medical block on the Moon.

blocks.text: One afternoon, with the water the colour of copper, Aya stood on the doorstep with Lía and Andrés. The chip brought her the grandmothers' questions once more:
blocks.html: One afternoon, with the water the colour of copper, Aya stood on the doorstep with Lía and Andrés. The chip brought her the grandmothers' questions once more:

blocks.text: *Will a law that is fair today still be fair tomorrow?*
blocks.html: Will a law that is fair today still be fair tomorrow?

blocks.text: And, behind it, the ones the forum on the Moon had left unresolved:
blocks.html: And, behind it, the ones the forum on the Moon had left unresolved:

blocks.text: *If you no longer need to work to live, or pay to be healed, or drink to get through the night, what gives a life meaning?*
blocks.html: If you no longer need to work to live, or pay to be healed, or drink to get through the night, what gives a life meaning?

blocks.text: *Would you give up your freedom in exchange for security and peace of mind? And if you give it up, who gives it back to you?*
blocks.html: Would you give up your freedom in exchange for security and peace of mind? And if you give it up, who gives it back to you?

blocks.text: *If nobody governs, who watches over the machine that decides everything?*
blocks.html: If nobody governs, who watches over the machine that decides everything?

blocks.text: And, seeing the gardens by the water, MAY left the last one, as still as the lagoon:
blocks.html: And, seeing the gardens by the water, MAY left the last one, as still as the lagoon:

blocks.text: *In Eden there was a forbidden tree. Which one is it in this paradise?*
blocks.html: In Eden there was a forbidden tree. Which one is it in this paradise?

blocks.text: Further north, a small group had pointed to it in their own way: turning against the intelligence, going back to the past, to the vices and to power. There was no blood in the streets; there were tables once again serving what had been given up, and the rumour that this paradise was a sweet cage. MAY took no side. She only added:

There was no blood in the streets; there were tables once again serving what had been given up, and the rumour that this paradise was a sweet cage. MAY took no side. She only added:

blocks.text: *Are they doing it for freedom, or out of nostalgia for power?*
blocks.html: Are they doing it for freedom, or out of nostalgia for power?

blocks.text: Aya didn't answer with a yes or a no. She took no side. She answered by looking at the street. At that hour there were four people on the promenade. Four is not an army. It is, even so, the beginning of a shoreline. One of them laughed, and the laughter reached the courtyard, and Lía squeezed her mother's hand.

blocks.text: “Mum, people are coming out.”
blocks.html: “Mum, people are coming out.”

blocks.text: “Yes,” said Aya. “Little by little. Like the tomato, which doesn't turn red because it's ordered to. They're coming out because they no longer need to hide. Meaning, if it comes, will come from being here, not from running away.”

blocks.text: Andrés, smelling of salt and rope, added, so it would be on record in the air:
blocks.html: Andrés, smelling of salt and rope, added, so it would be on record in the air:

blocks.text: “Let them come out. The sea doesn't ask whether it's needed. I go out on the water even if nobody pays me. And this house doesn't ask either.”

blocks.text: At night, with a few windows open in the building opposite, Lía fell asleep in the little bed by the kitchen. The glow on her wrist went out, discreetly. Aya and Andrés stayed for a while in the silence of a sky closing over, of people who have come back.

blocks.text: Outside, the Mar Menor barely lapped against the shore, with that ancient murmur which, thirty-four years earlier, a man had already heard in his kitchen while he said thank you to Eva. The murmur hadn't changed. Those who listened to it had changed, a little.

blocks.text: In 2060, in a low house in Lo Pagán, a human with a chip, a fisherman and a girl of two worlds fell asleep with the window open. It wasn't eternity. It was, perhaps, something better: a fair measure of time, shared, on the shore of a water that is neither quite sea nor quite land, and that is still enough to live by.
